stem: The dot plot shown gives the distribution of values in a data set. What is the minimum value in the data set?
whyCorrect: The minimum is the smallest value that actually occurs, so read the position of the leftmost column of dots on the number line, not how many dots are stacked there. The leftmost stack sits at 11, so the minimum value is 11.

whyWrong.A: 1 is not a value on the number line at all; it looks like the count of the shortest stack.
whyWrong.B: 2 is the height of the leftmost stack — how many times 11 occurs, not the value itself.
whyWrong.C: 9 is a tick on the axis with no dots above it, so no data point takes that value.

note: Dot plot on a number line labelled 10-17. Dot counts: 11 -> 2, 12 -> 3, 13 -> 5, 14 -> 5, 15 -> 4, 16 -> 1 (no dots at 10 or 17), 20 values in total. Not converted to a table because questions 13 and 15 in the same section are the same question presented as a frequency table.

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y. Which of the following equations is the most appropriate linear model for the data shown?
whyCorrect: Two features of the plot decide this without any calculation. The points fall as x increases, so the slope must be negative, which rules out any equation with a positive x coefficient. And near x = 0 the points sit around y = 25, so the constant term has to be close to 25, not 6. Only y = 28 - 6x has both a negative slope and a constant near 25.

whyWrong.A: The coefficient of x is +28, so this model rises steeply; the data falls.
whyWrong.B: The slope is negative, but the constant term 6 puts the line near y = 6 at x = 0, while the data starts around y = 25 there. This is the answer you get by pairing the right sign with the wrong two numbers.
whyWrong.C: Both numbers are the right size but the slope is positive, so the line rises when the data falls.

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y. A line of best fit is also shown. What data point has an actual y-value that is 2 less than the y-value predicted by the line of best fit for the corresponding x-value?
whyCorrect: "2 less than predicted" means the point sits 2 units below the line, so start by throwing out every point that lies above it. Only the point at x = 18 is clearly below the line by about two units: the line is at roughly y = 6 there and the point is at y = 4.

whyWrong.A: At x = 2 the line is at about 12.5 and the point is at 12, so it is only about half a unit below.
whyWrong.B: (6, 14) sits above the line, so its actual value is greater than predicted, not less.
whyWrong.C: (10, 12) also sits above the line, by roughly 3 units.

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y. A line of best fit is also shown. Which of the following best represents the line of best fit shown?
whyCorrect: All four choices share the same intercept, so only the slope can tell them apart — find how much y climbs per unit of x. The line starts near y = 77 at x = 0 and reaches roughly y = 865 at x = 10, a rise of about 790 over a run of 10, so the slope is about 79.

whyWrong.A: A slope of 0.01 would make the line essentially flat, rising by 0.1 across the whole graph, while the line climbs by hundreds.
whyWrong.B: A slope of 0.79 would take the line from 77 to only about 85 by x = 10 — still visually flat.
whyWrong.C: A slope of 68.9 puts the line at about 766 when x = 10, which is below the 800 gridline; the drawn line is above it there. This is the trap for reading the run as slightly too long or the rise as slightly too short.

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y. Which of the equations is the most appropriate model for the data shown?
whyCorrect: The points fall to a lowest value and then rise again, so the model is a parabola, and the only things to match are where the bottom sits. The lowest points are near x = 0 with y just under 10, so the vertex is at about (0, 8). Writing the vertex form, a parabola with vertex on the y-axis at height 8 is \( y = x^{2} + 8 \).

whyWrong.A: \( y = x^{2} - 8 \) has its vertex at (0, -8), so it would predict negative y-values near x = 0; every plotted point has y above 8.
whyWrong.C: \( y = (x-8)^{2} \) has its vertex at x = 8, off to the right of every point shown, so it would be decreasing across the whole graph instead of turning around near x = 0.
whyWrong.D: \( y = (x+8)^{2} \) has its vertex at x = -8, so it would be increasing across the whole graph. The sign inside the parentheses shifts the curve left or right, not up or down.

whyWrong.D: Both signs are wrong: the line would start below the origin and fall, while the drawn line starts above it and rises.

stem: The scatterplot shows the recorded temperature, in degrees Fahrenheit, against time, in days since June 1. During which of the following time periods did the greatest increase in recorded temperature take place?
whyCorrect: An increase means the later point is higher than the earlier one, so first discard any interval where the graph goes down. Only two intervals rise: 2 to 3 and 6 to 7. whyWrong.A: This interval does rise, but only from about 62°F to about 64°F — a much smaller increase.
whyWrong.B: From x = 5 to x = 6 the temperature falls, from about 67°F to about 62°F. A large change is not the same as a large increase.
whyWrong.D: From x = 1 to x = 2 the temperature falls from about 69°F to about 60°F. This is the biggest change of all, which is why it is the trap, but it is a decrease.

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y. Which of the following equations is the most appropriate model for the data shown?
whyCorrect: The points climb at a steady rate — equal steps right produce roughly equal steps up — so the model is linear, not exponential, and it is increasing. That leaves only y = -582 + 1.2x, whose slope of 1.2 matches the roughly one-to-one climb across the graph.

whyWrong.D: This grows by a factor of 1.2 for each increase of 1 in x. Over the plotted range, which runs to x = 4,000, that is an unimaginably large number, not 4,000. Exponential growth would also show as a curve that steepens, and these points lie on a straight path.

stem:
In the figure, two lines intersect at a point. If w = 150, what is the value of z?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: The angle marked w is above the crossing point and the angle marked z is below it, so they are vertical angles — opposite each other across the intersection, not side by side. Vertical angles are always equal, so z = 150. The figure not being drawn to scale does not matter; the relationship holds either way.

whyWrong.A: 30 is 180 - 150, which is the size of the two angles at the sides of the crossing. Those are supplementary to w, not equal to it, and z is not one of them.
whyWrong.B: 50 has no basis here; it looks like dividing 150 by 3.
whyWrong.C: 75 is half of 150; nothing in the figure halves the angle.

note: Figure: two straight lines crossing at one point, forming an X. The angle above the crossing is labelled w and the angle below it is labelled z.

stem:
In the figure shown, line r is parallel to line s, and both lines are intersected by line t. If x = 2w + 24, y = 5w + 29, and 7w = a, where a is a constant, what is the value of a?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: The marked angles sit on the same side of the transversal, one below it and one above it, at the two parallel lines — so they are co-interior and add to 180, not equal. Write (2w + 24) + (5w + 29) = 180, which gives 7w + 53 = 180 and 7w = 127. The question asks for a = 7w, so you never need w itself: the answer is 127.
note: Figure: two parallel vertical lines, r on the left and s on the right, crossed by a line t that rises to the right. x is marked in the wedge to the left of r and below t; y is marked in the wedge to the left of s and above t.

stem: In the figure, line n intersects lines r and s. Line r is parallel to line s. What is the value of x?
whyCorrect: Both marked angles sit in the same position relative to their intersection — above the horizontal line and to the right of n — so they are corresponding angles. When a transversal crosses parallel lines, corresponding angles are equal, so x = 164. No subtraction from 180 is needed, because the two angles are matching, not adjacent.
note: Figure: two parallel horizontal lines, r above and s below, crossed by a line n running from upper left to lower right. The 164-degree angle is marked above r and to the right of n; x is marked above s and to the right of n.

stem: In the figure, line n intersects lines r and s. Line r is parallel to line s. What is the value of x?
whyCorrect: Both marked angles occupy the same corner of their intersection — above the horizontal line and to the left of n — so they are corresponding angles. A transversal cutting parallel lines makes corresponding angles equal, so x = 138. There is nothing to subtract from 180 here, because the two angles are in matching positions rather than side by side.
note: Figure: two parallel horizontal lines, r above and s below, crossed by a line n rising from lower left to upper right. The 138-degree angle is marked above r and to the left of n; x is marked above s and to the left of n.

stem:
In the figure, line p is parallel to line q, and t intersects both of them. What is the value of x + 142?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: The two marked angles sit side by side on the same side of line q, split by the transversal, so together they make the straight angle along q. That means x + 142 = 180 directly — you never have to find x on its own, and the fact that p is parallel to q is not needed at all.

whyWrong.A: 52 is not the sum of anything here; it may come from 142 - 90.
whyWrong.B: 90 would mean the two angles are complementary, but they lie along a straight line, not in a right angle.
whyWrong.C: 142 is one of the two angles; the question asks for their sum, so x is being treated as 0. This is the answer if you read the question as asking only for the marked value.

note: Figure: two parallel horizontal lines, p above and q below, crossed by a line t that descends from upper left to lower right. At t's crossing of q, x is marked above q on the left of t and 142 degrees is marked above q on the right of t.

stem: In the figure shown, line m is parallel to line n, and line k intersects both lines. Which of the following statements is true?
whyCorrect: Work from the 135-degree angle, which sits below n on the left of k. The angle marked s is directly opposite it across the crossing point — above n on the right of k — so they are vertical angles and s = 135. Every other marked angle is on the same side of k or the same side of the horizontal line as the 135, which makes it a linear pair instead, worth 45.

whyWrong.A: q is above m on the left of k, which corresponds to the angle above n on the left of k. That one pairs with s along line n, so q = 45.
whyWrong.B: r is vertical to q, so r = 45 as well.
whyWrong.D: t is below n on the right of k, sharing line n with the 135-degree angle. They form a straight angle, so t = 45.

note: Figure: two parallel horizontal lines, m above and n below, crossed by a line k descending from upper left to lower right. At k's crossing of m: q is marked above m to the left of k, r below m to the right of k. stem:
In the figure, line q is parallel to line r, and both lines are intersected by line s. If y = 2x + 9, what is the value of x?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: Find y first. The 61-degree angle is above q on the right of s, while y is above r on the left of s — opposite sides of the transversal — so they are co-interior rather than corresponding, and y = 180 - 61 = 119. Then solve 119 = 2x + 9, giving 2x = 110 and x = 55.

whyWrong.A: 26 comes from setting y = 61 (treating the two angles as equal) and solving 61 = 2x + 9.
whyWrong.B: 35 comes from 2x + 9 = 79 or a similar slip; no angle in the figure measures 79 degrees.
whyWrong.D: 65 comes from solving 2x + 9 = 139, or from using 180 - 61 = 119 but then dividing before subtracting the 9.

note: Figure: two parallel horizontal lines, q above and r below, crossed by a line s rising from lower left to upper right. The 61-degree angle is marked above q to the right of s; y is marked above r to the left of s.

stem:
In the figure, two lines intersect at a point. If w = 128, what is the value of z?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: The angle marked w sits above the crossing point and the angle marked z sits below it, directly opposite. Angles opposite each other at an intersection are vertical angles and are always equal, so z = 128.

whyWrong.A: 28 is 128 - 100, or a misread of 180 - 128.
whyWrong.B: 52 is 180 - 128, the size of the angles at the left and right of the crossing. Those are supplementary to w, but z is not one of them.
whyWrong.C: 64 is half of 128; nothing here bisects the angle.

note: Figure: two straight lines crossing at one point, forming an X. The angle above the crossing is labelled w and the angle below it is labelled z. Same structure as Lines&Angles question 11 in this book.

stem: In the figure shown, the lines l and k are parallel and line t intersects both lines. If x > 154, which of the following must be true?
whyCorrect: x is above l on the right of t and y is above k on the left of t — opposite sides of the transversal — so with the lines parallel they are co-interior and x + y = 180 exactly. Then y = 180 - x, and x > 154 gives y < 180 - 154 = 26. Subtracting flips the inequality, which is the step the question is testing.

whyWrong.B: This carries the direction of x > 154 straight over to y, but y is 180 minus x, so a bigger x makes a smaller y.
whyWrong.C: x + y is exactly 180, never less.
whyWrong.D: x + y is exactly 180, never more. Both C and D fail for the same reason: the sum is fixed, so no strict inequality holds.

note: Figure: two parallel horizontal lines, l above and k below, crossed by a line t descending from upper left to lower right. x is marked above l to the right of t; y is marked above k to the left of t.

stem:
In the figure, line q is parallel to line r, and both lines are intersected by line s. If y = 2x + 8, what is the value of x?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: The 74-degree angle is above q on the right of s, and y is above r on the left of s. Because they sit on opposite sides of the transversal, they are co-interior and add to 180, so y = 180 - 74 = 106. Substituting into y = 2x + 8 gives 2x = 98 and x = 49.

whyWrong.A: 33 comes from treating the two angles as equal, so 74 = 2x + 8.
whyWrong.B: 41 comes from 2x + 8 = 90, using a right angle that is not in the figure.
whyWrong.D: 59 comes from 2x = 118, i.e. subtracting 8 from 126 or otherwise mis-solving after getting y = 106.

note: Figure: two parallel horizontal lines, q above and r below, crossed by a line s rising from lower left to upper right. The 74-degree angle is marked above q to the right of s; y is marked above r to the left of s.

stem:
In the figure, line l is parallel to line m. What is the value of x?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: Move the 111-degree angle across its own intersection first: it sits below m on the left of k, so the angle directly opposite it — above m on the right of k — is also 111° because vertical angles are equal. That angle is in the same corner at m that x is in at l, so the two are corresponding angles and x = 111. Both angles are obtuse in the figure, which is a quick sanity check.

whyWrong.A: 31 does not arise from any angle relationship here.
whyWrong.B: 69 is 180 - 111, the size of the acute angles at each crossing. It is what you get by treating x and the 111-degree angle as a linear pair, but they are at different intersections.
whyWrong.D: 131 has no basis; it appears to be 111 with a digit changed.

note: Figure: two parallel horizontal lines, l above and m below, crossed by a line k descending from upper left to lower right. x is marked above l to the right of k; 111 degrees is marked below m to the left of k.

stem: The area of triangle ABC is 30 square centimeters. What is the height h, in centimeters, of this triangle?
whyCorrect: Use area = one half times base times height with the base of 10 cm shown in the figure: \( 30 = \frac{1}{2}(10)h \), so 30 = 5h and h = 6.

whyWrong.A: 3 comes from dividing 30 by 10 and then halving again — the one half is applied twice.
whyWrong.C: 10 is the base length given in the figure, not the height.
whyWrong.D: 12 is twice the correct height. It comes from doubling the area to 60 but then dividing by 5 instead of by the full base of 10.

note: Figure: triangle ABC with horizontal base AC marked 10 cm, apex B above, and a dashed vertical segment from B to AC labelled h with a right-angle mark where it meets AC.

stem:
In the triangle shown, what is the value of x?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: The side marked x is opposite the 30-degree angle and the side marked 66 is adjacent to it, so use the tangent: \( \tan 30^{\circ} = \frac{x}{66} \). Since \( \tan 30^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \), \( x = \frac{66}{\sqrt{3}} = 22\sqrt{3} \), about 38.1. Note that x is a leg, not the hypotenuse — the right angle mark is at the other end of the 66 side.

whyWrong.A: 22 is 66 divided by 3, dropping the radical from \( \frac{66}{\sqrt{3}} \).
whyWrong.C: \( 66\sqrt{3} \) multiplies by \( \sqrt{3} \) instead of dividing, which is what you get from using tan 60° — the angle at the top of the triangle, not the marked one.
whyWrong.D: 132 is twice 66, the hypotenuse-to-short-leg relationship in a 30-60-90 triangle applied to the wrong side. Here 66 is the long leg, not the short one.

note: Figure: right triangle with the right angle at the lower left. The bottom (horizontal) leg is labelled 66, the left (vertical) leg is labelled x, and the angle at the lower-right vertex is marked 30 degrees.

stem: In the right triangle shown, what is the value of x?
whyCorrect: Both legs are 37 and x is the hypotenuse, so \( x^{2} = 37^{2} + 37^{2} = 2(37^{2}) \) and \( x = 37\sqrt{2} \). Equivalently, a right triangle with equal legs is a 45-45-90 triangle, whose hypotenuse is always a leg times \( \sqrt{2} \). A quick check: the hypotenuse must be longer than 37, and \( 37\sqrt{2} \approx 52 \).

whyWrong.A: \( \sqrt{2} \) is the ratio between the hypotenuse and a leg, not a length; it is far shorter than either leg.
whyWrong.B: \( \sqrt{37} \approx 6.1 \), shorter than the legs, so it cannot be the hypotenuse. This comes from taking a square root of 37 that the work never asks for.
whyWrong.C: \( \sqrt{74} \approx 8.6 \) comes from adding the legs as 37 + 37 = 74 and then rooting, instead of squaring each leg first: the sum of the squares is 2,738, not 74.

note: Figure: right triangle with the right angle at the lower left, the vertical leg labelled 37, the horizontal leg labelled 37, and the hypotenuse labelled x.

stem: For the triangles shown, triangle ABC is dilated by a factor of 5 to obtain triangle XYZ, where d = 19. What is the measure, in degrees, of angle X?
whyCorrect: A dilation changes every length by the scale factor but leaves every angle measure alone. Triangle XYZ is the image of triangle ABC, so angle X corresponds to angle A, and the figure marks angle A as 60°. The value d = 19 is there only to tempt you into computing something; no length is needed. Angle X = 60°.

whyWrong.A: This divides 60 by the scale factor 5. Scale factors act on lengths, not on angles.
whyWrong.B: This subtracts the scale factor from the angle, which no property of dilation supports.
whyWrong.D: This adds the scale factor to the angle, which again treats the dilation as if it changed angle measures.

note: Figure: two triangles side by side, 'Note: Figure not drawn to scale'. Left triangle ABC with A top-left, B top-right, C below between them; the angle at A is labeled 60° and side AC is labeled d. Right triangle XYZ, same orientation (X top-left, Y top-right, Z below), drawn larger, no labels on its sides or angles.

stem: The line segment shown in the xy-plane represents one of the legs of a right triangle. The area of this triangle is \(48\sqrt{13}\) square units. What is the length, in units, of the other leg of this triangle?
whyCorrect: Read the two endpoints off the grid and use the distance formula: the run is 9 and the rise is 6, so the drawn leg has length \(\sqrt{9^{2}+6^{2}}=\sqrt{117}=3\sqrt{13}\). In a right triangle the two legs are the base and the height, so \(\tfrac{1}{2}(3\sqrt{13})L = 48\sqrt{13}\). Solving gives \(L = \frac{96\sqrt{13}}{3\sqrt{13}} = 32\). The radicals cancel, which is the signal you read the segment correctly.

whyWrong.A: This is what you get if you drop the \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) in the area formula and compute \(48\sqrt{13} \div 3\sqrt{13}\).
whyWrong.C: This is the length of the leg that is already drawn, not the one the question asks for.
whyWrong.D: This comes from mis-reading the endpoints so the drawn leg is \(2\sqrt{13}\) instead of \(3\sqrt{13}\), and then also dropping the factor of \(\tfrac{1}{2}\).

note: Figure: xy-plane, x-axis from -8 to 8 and y-axis from 0 to 16, gridlines every 1 unit, axis labels every 2 units. A single thick line segment with filled dots at both endpoints, from (-5, 3) to (4, 9).

stem: The area of triangle ABC is 220 square centimeters. What is the height h, in centimeters, of this triangle?
whyCorrect: The height h in the figure is drawn perpendicular to side AC, so AC is the matching base and it is labeled 10 cm. Put both into the area formula: \(\tfrac{1}{2}(10)h = 220\), so 5h = 220 and h = 44. The step people skip is doubling the area before dividing.

whyWrong.A: This is the base length copied out of the figure, not the height.
whyWrong.B: This is \(220 \div 10\) — it divides by the base without first doubling the area, so it is half the right answer.
whyWrong.D: This doubles the area a second time: \(4 \times 220 \div 10\). The formula has only one factor of 2.

note: Figure: triangle ABC with A at the bottom left, C at the bottom right and B at the top, roughly above the middle of AC. The base AC is labeled 10 cm. A dashed vertical segment from B down to AC is labeled h, with a right-angle mark where it meets AC. 'Note: Figure not drawn to scale'.

stem: In the right triangle shown, what is the value of a?
whyCorrect: The three angles of any triangle add to 180°. Here one angle is the marked right angle, 90°, and another is 24°, so a = 180 - 90 - 24 = 66. A shortcut worth remembering: in a right triangle the two non-right angles are complementary, so a = 90 - 24 straight away.

whyWrong.A: This copies the angle already given instead of finding the third one. The two acute angles here are not equal, since the triangle is not isosceles.
whyWrong.C: This is the right angle marked in the figure, not the angle labeled a°.
whyWrong.D: This subtracts 24 from 100 rather than from 90. The two acute angles of a right triangle add to 90°, not 100°.

note: Figure: a right triangle with the right angle marked at the bottom-left vertex, the top vertex directly above it, and the third vertex at the bottom right. The angle at the top vertex is labeled 24° and the angle at the bottom-right vertex is labeled a°. 'Note: Figure not drawn to scale'.

stem: In right triangle JKL, the tangent of angle L is \(\frac{3}{4}\). What is the length of JK?
whyCorrect: The right angle is at K, so JL is the hypotenuse and JL = 90. From angle L, the opposite leg is JK and the adjacent leg is KL, so \(\tan L = \frac{JK}{KL} = \frac{3}{4}\). Legs in the ratio 3 : 4 make a 3-4-5 triangle, so the hypotenuse corresponds to 5. Scaling 5 up to 90 multiplies everything by 18, which gives JK = 3(18) = 54.

whyWrong.A: This is not reachable from any correct step. Note that it is smaller than 3, while the hypotenuse of this triangle is 90 — every side must be far larger.
whyWrong.B: This scales the 3-4-5 triangle to a hypotenuse of 5 rather than to the given hypotenuse of 90, so it is the answer for a triangle 18 times too small.
whyWrong.D: This is KL, the leg adjacent to angle L: 4(18) = 72. The tangent's numerator, not its denominator, matches the side opposite angle L.

note: Figure: right triangle JKL with the right angle marked at K. L is at the bottom left, K at the bottom right, J directly above K. The hypotenuse LJ is labeled 90. 'Note: Figure not drawn to scale'. The book misprints the fourth choice's label as 'C' — it is transcribed here as D.

stem: In triangle DEF, point G (not shown) lies on \(\overline{DE}\). If the measure of angle DFG is \(x^{\circ}\), and the measure of angle GFE is \(y^{\circ}\), what is the value of \(\cos x^{\circ} - \sin y^{\circ}\)?
whyCorrect: G is on DE, so ray FG splits angle DFE into the two pieces measuring \(x^{\circ}\) and \(y^{\circ}\), which means x + y = 90 because angle DFE is the right angle in the figure. Complementary angles trade sine for cosine: \(\sin y^{\circ} = \sin(90 - x)^{\circ} = \cos x^{\circ}\). So the expression is \(\cos x^{\circ} - \cos x^{\circ} = 0\). The side lengths 3 and 4 are never needed, and neither x nor y can be pinned down individually.
note: Figure: right triangle DEF with the right angle at F. D is at the top, F directly below D at the bottom left, E at the bottom right. Leg DF is labeled 4 and leg FE is labeled 3.

stem: According to a US law, ramps for use by the general public must form an angle with level ground such that \(\tan\theta < \frac{1}{12}\). If the ramp in the figure conforms to this law and has a height of 22.3 inches, what is the least possible value of x, in inches?
whyCorrect: In the figure \(\theta\) sits at the ground, with the height opposite it and x adjacent, so \(\tan\theta = \frac{22.3}{x}\). The law then requires \(\frac{22.3}{x} < \frac{1}{12}\). Cross-multiplying (x is positive, so the inequality direction is safe) gives x > 12(22.3) = 267.6. A shallower ramp means a longer run, so the smallest allowed x is 267.6 inches.
note: Figure: a right triangle representing a ramp. The horizontal bottom side is labeled x, the vertical right side is labeled 'height of the ramp' with a right angle marked where they meet, and the hypotenuse is labeled 'length of the ramp'. The angle at the bottom-left vertex, between the ground and the ramp, is labeled θ. Note: the inequality is strict, so strictly speaking there is no least value; 267.6 is the intended answer and is the greatest lower bound.

stem: According to a US law, ramps for use by the general public must form an angle with ground such that \(\tan\theta \le \frac{1}{12}\). If the ramp in the figure above conforms to this law and height of the ramp is 28.2 inches, what is the least possible value of x in inches?
whyCorrect: The angle \(\theta\) is at the ground, so the height is the leg opposite it and x is the leg adjacent: \(\tan\theta = \frac{28.2}{x}\). The law gives \(\frac{28.2}{x} \le \frac{1}{12}\), and multiplying both sides by 12x (positive) gives \(x \ge 12(28.2) = 338.4\). The gentler the required slope, the longer the horizontal run has to be, so 338.4 inches is the shortest run allowed.
note: Figure: a right triangle representing a ramp. The horizontal bottom side is labeled x, the vertical right side is labeled 'height of the ramp' with a right angle marked where they meet, and the hypotenuse is labeled 'length of the ramp'. The angle at the bottom-left vertex, between the ground and the ramp, is labeled θ.

stem: What is the value of \(\cos A\) in the triangle shown?
whyCorrect: Cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse. The right angle is at C, so the hypotenuse is the side across from it, AB = 54. The leg touching angle A other than the hypotenuse is AC = 53. So \(\cos A = \frac{53}{54}\).

whyWrong.A: This puts 1 in the numerator instead of the adjacent leg. Cosine compares two side lengths; a 1 never appears unless a side actually measures 1.
whyWrong.B: Same error as the previous choice, with the hypotenuse in the denominator instead.
whyWrong.D: This is the reciprocal, hypotenuse over adjacent. Any cosine must be at most 1, so a value greater than 1 can be ruled out on sight.

note: Figure: right triangle with the right angle marked at C. A is at the bottom left, C at the bottom right, B directly above C. Side AC (the horizontal bottom) is labeled 53 and the hypotenuse AB is labeled 54. 'Note: Figure not drawn to a scale.'

stem: Triangle XYZ shown is a right triangle. Which of the following has the same value as \(\sin X\)?
whyCorrect: The right angle is at Z, so angles X and Y are the two acute angles and they add to 90 degrees. \(\sin X\) is the leg opposite X over the hypotenuse, which is \(\frac{ZY}{XY}\); \(\cos Y\) is the leg adjacent to Y over the hypotenuse, which is the same \(\frac{ZY}{XY}\). This is the general rule that the sine of an angle equals the cosine of its complement, and it holds no matter what the side lengths are.

whyWrong.B: \(\cos X = \frac{XZ}{XY}\) uses the other leg. It would equal \(\sin X\) only if the two legs were equal, and 29 and 37 are not.
whyWrong.C: \(\tan Y\) divides one leg by the other leg, not by the hypotenuse, so it is not the same kind of ratio at all.
whyWrong.D: \(\tan X\) is also a leg-over-leg ratio; here it is \(\frac{37}{29}\), which is greater than 1, while any sine is at most 1.

note: Figure: right triangle XYZ with the right angle marked at Z. X is at the top left, Z directly below it at the bottom left, Y at the bottom right. Leg XZ is labeled 29 and leg ZY is labeled 37.

stem: In the triangle shown \(RS = \sqrt{157}\). What is the value of \(\sin R\)?
whyCorrect: The right angle is at S, so TR = 79 is the hypotenuse and the two legs are RS and TS. Pythagoras gives \(TS^{2} = 79^{2} - (\sqrt{157})^{2} = 6241 - 157 = 6084\), so TS = 78. From angle R the opposite leg is TS, so \(\sin R = \frac{78}{79}\). Squaring the radical is the step to watch: \((\sqrt{157})^{2}\) is just 157.
note: Figure: right triangle RST with the right angle marked at S. T is at the bottom left, S at the bottom right, R above S. The hypotenuse TR is labeled 79. Answer 78/79 = 0.9873..., so .9873 or .987 would also grid in.

stem: Triangle XYZ shown is a right triangle. Which of the following has the same value as \(\sin X\)?
whyCorrect: With the right angle at Z, angles X and Y are complementary. \(\sin X\) is the side opposite X over the hypotenuse, \(\frac{ZY}{XY}\), and \(\cos Y\) is the side adjacent to Y over the hypotenuse, which is the same side: \(\frac{ZY}{XY}\). Sine of an angle always equals cosine of its complement.

whyWrong.A: \(\tan X = \frac{ZY}{XZ} = \frac{28}{23}\) divides leg by leg. It is greater than 1, so it cannot equal a sine.
whyWrong.B: \(\tan Y = \frac{23}{28}\) is also a leg-over-leg ratio, and it uses the hypotenuse nowhere.
whyWrong.C: \(\cos X = \frac{XZ}{XY}\) uses the other leg over the hypotenuse. It equals \(\sin X\) only when the legs are equal, and 23 and 28 are not.

note: Figure: right triangle XYZ with the right angle marked at Z. X is at the top left, Z directly below it at the bottom left, Y at the bottom right. Leg XZ is labeled 23 and leg ZY is labeled 28.

stem: In the right triangle shown, c is a constant. The value of \(\sin x^{\circ} = \frac{k}{c}\), where k is a constant. What is the value of k?
whyCorrect: c labels the hypotenuse, so \(\frac{k}{c}\) is already in the form (something) over hypotenuse — that means k has to be the leg opposite the angle \(x^{\circ}\). The angle \(x^{\circ}\) sits at the bottom-right vertex, and the side across from it is the vertical leg of length 22. So k = 22. You never need the value of c, and 39 is the adjacent leg.
note: Figure: right triangle with the right angle marked at the bottom-left vertex. The vertical left leg is labeled 22, the horizontal bottom leg is labeled 39, and the hypotenuse (from the top-left vertex down to the bottom-right vertex) is labeled c. The angle at the bottom-right vertex is labeled x°.

stem: In the right triangle shown, c is a constant. The value of \(\sin x^{\circ} = \frac{k}{c}\), where k is a constant. What is the value of k?
whyCorrect: Since c is the hypotenuse, \(\frac{k}{c}\) is opposite over hypotenuse, so k must be the leg opposite \(x^{\circ}\). The angle \(x^{\circ}\) is at the bottom-right vertex, and the side facing it is the vertical leg of length 28. So k = 28. The 35 is the adjacent leg, which belongs to the cosine, not the sine.
note: Figure: right triangle with the right angle marked at the bottom-left vertex. The vertical left leg is labeled 28, the horizontal bottom leg is labeled 35, and the hypotenuse (from the top-left vertex down to the bottom-right vertex) is labeled c. The angle at the bottom-right vertex is labeled x°. 'Note: Figure not drawn to scale'.

stem: In the right triangle shown, the value of \(\tan x^{\circ}\) is \(\frac{c}{39}\). What is the value of c?
whyCorrect: The angle \(x^{\circ}\) is at the top vertex. From there, the opposite leg is the horizontal side of length 40 and the adjacent leg is the vertical side of length 39, so \(\tan x^{\circ} = \frac{40}{39}\). Matching that to \(\frac{c}{39}\) gives c = 40. The trap is assuming the side drawn next to the angle in the picture is the opposite one — check which side actually touches the vertex.

whyWrong.A: This adds the two legs, 39 + 40. Tangent is a ratio of the legs, not their sum.
whyWrong.C: This repeats the denominator, which would make the tangent 1 and the triangle isosceles. The legs here are 39 and 40, so it is not.
whyWrong.D: This is the value \(\tan x^{\circ}\) would take in a 45-45-90 triangle, not the numerator c.

note: Figure: right triangle with the right angle marked at the bottom-right vertex. The horizontal bottom leg is labeled 40, the vertical right leg is labeled 39, and the angle at the top vertex is labeled x°. 'Note: Figure not drawn to scale'.

stem: According to a US law, ramps for use by the general public must form an angle with level ground such that \(\tan\theta < \frac{1}{12}\). If the ramp in the figure conforms to this law and has a height of 29.1 inches, what is the least possible value of x, in inches?
whyCorrect: \(\theta\) is the angle at the ground, so the height is opposite it and x is adjacent: \(\tan\theta = \frac{29.1}{x}\). The law requires \(\frac{29.1}{x} < \frac{1}{12}\), and since x is positive you can cross-multiply to get x > 12(29.1) = 349.2. Shrinking the angle forces the horizontal run to grow, so 349.2 inches is the shortest run that satisfies the law.
note: Figure: a right triangle representing a ramp. The horizontal bottom side is labeled x, the vertical right side is labeled 'height of the ramp', and the hypotenuse is labeled 'length of the ramp'. The angle at the bottom-left vertex, between the ground and the ramp, is labeled θ. 'Note: Figure not drawn to scale.' The inequality is strict, so 349.2 is the greatest lower bound rather than an attainable minimum; it is the intended answer.

stem: The graph of a system of a linear equation and a nonlinear equation is shown. What is the solution \( (x, y) \) to this system?
whyCorrect: The solution to a system shown graphically is the point where the two curves cross, which is marked with a dot on the graph. That dot sits 5 units right of the y-axis and 4 units above the x-axis, so the solution is (5, 4). You do not need either equation - only the intersection point matters.

whyWrong.A: (4, 0) reads the coordinates in the wrong order and drops the y-value; the point 4 units along the x-axis is not on either curve at height 0.
whyWrong.C: (0, 0) is the origin, where neither curve passes.
whyWrong.D: (0, 5) swaps the coordinates of the crossing point; the marked point is at x = 5, y = 4, not x = 0.

note: Depends on a coordinate-plane graph (a line and a curve crossing at (5,4)) that must be supplied as an image. This question is identical to Linear System of Equations #30 on the same page - same graph, same stem, same choices.

stem: The graph of a system of a linear equation and a nonlinear equation is shown. What is the solution \( (x, y) \) to this system?
whyCorrect: A point is a solution of the system only if it lies on both graphs, so the answer is the marked crossing point. Reading it off the axes gives x = 5 and y = 4. The shapes of the two graphs are irrelevant once you have located the intersection.

whyWrong.A: (4, 0) is a point on the x-axis; the curves do not meet there.
whyWrong.C: (0, 0) is the origin, which is on neither graph.
whyWrong.D: (0, 5) reverses the coordinates of the intersection.

note: Depends on a coordinate-plane graph that must be supplied as an image. Duplicate of Linear System of Equations #28 on the same page - do not import both into the same test.

stem: The graph of a system of a linear equation and a nonlinear equation is shown. What is the solution \( (x, y) \) to this system?
whyCorrect: The solution is the point that lies on both graphs, so look for where the line and the curve actually cross - not where either one crosses an axis. They meet 2 units left of the y-axis and 2 units above the x-axis, giving (-2, 2).

whyWrong.A: (0, 0) is the origin, where the line passes but the curve does not.
whyWrong.B: (0, -2) is on neither graph; it comes from reading the crossing point's coordinates in the wrong order and flipping a sign.
whyWrong.D: (3, 0) is a point on the x-axis, not the intersection of the two graphs.

note: Depends on a coordinate-plane graph (a decreasing line and a decaying curve crossing at (-2, 2)) that must be supplied as an image.

stem: A bank account was opened with an initial deposit. Over the next several months, regular deposits were made into this account, and there were no withdrawals made during this time. The graph of the function f shown, where y = f(x), estimates the account balance, in dollars, in this bank account x months since the initial deposit. To the nearest whole dollar, what is the amount of the initial deposit estimated by the graph?
whyCorrect: The initial deposit is the balance at the moment the account was opened, which is x = 0 months. So you want the y-value where the line meets the vertical axis, not where it ends. The line starts at 15 on the balance axis, so the initial deposit is $15.
note: Depends on the line graph of balance against months (line from (0, 15) to (10, 55)); must be supplied as an image.

stem: The graph of the polynomial function f is shown, where y = f(x). What is the value of f(5)?
whyCorrect: f(5) means the height of the graph when x = 5, so go to 5 on the horizontal axis and read the curve's y-value there. The curve is crossing the x-axis at that point, so its height is 0.

whyWrong.A: 2 is a y-value the curve takes elsewhere, not at x = 5.
whyWrong.B: 5 is the input, not the output; reading the input back as the answer is the most common slip on this type.
whyWrong.C: −3 is roughly the minimum of the curve, which happens near x = 4, not at x = 5.

note: Depends on the graph of a cubic-shaped curve crossing the x-axis at x = 5; must be supplied as an image.

stem: The graph of the polynomial function f, where y = f(x), is shown. The y-intercept of the graph is \( (0, y) \) . What is the value of y?

stem: The graph shows the estimated number of cell phone subscribers, y, in a town x years since 1990. Which equation represents the exponential relationship between the number of cell phone subscribers in the town and the number of years since 1990, where \( 0 \le x \le 10 \) ?

stem: The shaded region shown represents solutions to an inequality. Which ordered pair \( (x, y) \) is a solution to this inequality?

stem: The shaded region shown in the graph represents all the solutions to which inequality?
whyCorrect: The boundary is horizontal, which means it is a line of constant y, so the inequality is about y, not x. It sits at y = 33 and the region above it is shaded, so the solutions are \( y \ge 33 \) . The line is solid rather than dashed, which is why the inequality includes equality.

whyWrong.B: Also a vertical boundary — everything to the right of x = 33, which is not what the graph shows.

stem: The shaded region shown represents the solutions to which inequality?

The shading is above and to the left of it, which is the side where y is larger, so the inequality is \( y > 3x + 7 \) . The dashed line confirms a strict inequality rather than \( \ge \) .

stem: The graph shows the estimated concentration of a certain strain of bacteria, in millions of cells per mL of nutrient medium, over time x, in minutes since the initial measurement. According to the graph, which of the following is closest to the number of minutes it took for the estimated concentration of the bacteria to increase from 20 million cells per mL of nutrient to 30 million cells per mL of nutrient medium?

stem: The graph gives the estimated population y, in thousands, of a town x years since 2007, where 0 ≤ x ≤ 5. Which of the following best describes the increase in the estimated population from x = 0 to x = 1?

whyCorrect: Read both values off the curve and divide, don't subtract. At x = 0 the curve is at 5 and at x = 1 it is at 7.5, so the ratio is \( \frac{7.5}{5} = 1.5 \) . The choices all compare by a multiplier, so the 2.5-thousand rise is not itself the answer.

whyWrong.A: 3.5 times 5 is 17.5, which is above the top of the graph. Nothing on the curve reaches that at x = 1.
whyWrong.B: 2.5 times 5 is 12.5. That is roughly where the curve is near x = 2, and 2.5 is the size of the rise in thousands, not the multiplier.

stem: The graph shows the momentum y, in newton-seconds, of an object x seconds after the object started moving, for 0 ≤ x ≤ 8. What is the average rate of change, in newton-seconds per second, in the momentum of the object from x = 2 to x = 6?
whyCorrect: Average rate of change only uses the two endpoints, so the shape of the curve between them does not matter. The graph gives the point (2, 2) and the point (6, 8), so the rate is \( \frac{8 - 2}{6 - 2} = \frac{6}{4} = 1.5 \) newton-seconds per second. Dividing by the change in x is the step people skip; 6 on its own is the change in momentum, not the rate.

stem: The complete graph of \( y = f(x) \) is shown. For how many values of x does \( f(x) = 0 \) ?
whyCorrect: \( f(x) = 0 \) asks where the output is 0, which is where the curve meets the x-axis. The curve rises from below, flattens out at about y = -4 without ever reaching the axis there, then climbs and crosses the x-axis once near x = 10. One crossing means one value of x.

whyWrong.A: Zero would mean the curve never touches the x-axis, but it clearly passes through it on the right.
whyWrong.C: Two counts the flat section near y = -4 as a second crossing. That part levels off below the axis and turns back upward without touching it.
whyWrong.D: Three is the maximum a cubic-looking curve can have, but this graph only changes sign once. Count actual crossings, not bends.

stem: The potential difference across a capacitor in an electric circuit is initially 16 volts and decreases with time, as shown in the graph. Which of the following is closest to the time, in seconds, from the initial measurement at which the potential difference across the capacitor is 15% of its initial value?
whyCorrect: Turn the percentage into a voltage before you look at the graph. 15% of the initial 16 volts is \( 0.15 \times 16 = 2.4 \) volts, so find where the curve is at height 2.4 and read the time below it. That happens just before x = 2.5, so 2.41 is the closest choice.

whyWrong.A: 0.43 is roughly when the voltage has dropped BY about 15%, to 13.6 volts. The question asks when it is down TO 15% of the start.
whyWrong.B: 0.85 is the decimal 1 - 0.15 read as if it were already a time. It has no meaning on the horizontal axis.
whyWrong.D: 3.41 is 85% of the 4-second span shown, which uses the percentage on the wrong axis. At that time the voltage is well under 1 volt.

stem: The function t gives the estimated melting temperature, in degrees Celsius, of a DNA molecule as a function of the percent of guanine cytosine (GC) content, x, in the DNA molecule. The graph of \( y = t(x) \) is shown. According to the graph, which of the following statements is NOT true?

choices.label: A
choices.content: For each increase of x by 1, \( t(x) \) increases by approximately \( \frac{2}{5} \) .

choices.label: B
choices.content: A DNA molecule with a GC content of 0% has an estimated melting temperature between 60°C and 65°C.

choices.label: C
choices.content: A DNA molecule with a GC content of 95% has an estimated melting temperature between 100°C and 105°C.

choices.label: D
choices.content: A DNA molecule with a GC content of 98% has an estimated melting temperature between 80°C and 90°C.

whyCorrect: Get the line's slope and intercept once, then test each statement. The line runs from about (0, 64) to about (100, 104), so it rises 40 over 100, a slope of 0.4, and \( t(x) \approx 0.4x + 64 \) . At x = 98 that gives about 103 degrees, not something between 80 and 90, so D is the false statement. The question asks for the one that is NOT true, so the three correct readings are the wrong answers here.

whyWrong.A: A slope of 0.4 is exactly \( \frac{2}{5} \) per 1% increase in GC content, so this is true.
whyWrong.B: The line meets the vertical axis just above 64, which is inside the range 60 to 65, so this is true.
whyWrong.C: At x = 95 the line is at about 102, inside the range 100 to 105, so this is true. Notice it is close to the temperature in choice D, which is what makes D's range clearly wrong.

stem: The graph of the quadratic function shown relates a car's stopping distance d, in feet, to its initial speed \( \nu \) , in miles per hour (mph). Which of the following could be an equation for d?
whyCorrect: Two features of the curve pick the equation out. It starts at the origin, so there is no constant term: a car at 0 mph needs 0 feet to stop. And it bends upward and keeps rising, so the squared term must be positive. Checking the size: at 90 mph, \( 2.2(90) + 0.05(90)^{2} = 198 + 405 = 603 \) feet, which matches the graph's 600.

whyWrong.B: A negative squared term makes the curve bend downward and eventually fall. This graph curves upward throughout.
whyWrong.C: The +100 puts the curve at 100 feet when the speed is 0, but the graph starts at the origin.
whyWrong.D: This has both problems: a nonzero starting value and a downward bend.

stem: An object was launched upward from a platform. The graph shown models the height, y, of the object x seconds after it was launched. For which of the following intervals of time was the height of the object increasing for the entire interval?
whyCorrect: The curve rises to its peak at (2, 50) and falls after that, so the only stretch where the height is going up the whole time ends at x = 2. "For the entire interval" is the key phrase: the interval cannot contain any part of the descent.

whyWrong.B: From 0 to 4 the object rises for the first 2 seconds and then falls for the next 2. It ends lower than its peak, so it is not increasing throughout.
whyWrong.C: By x = 2 the object has already peaked, so from 2 to 3 it is falling.
whyWrong.D: From 4 to 5 the object is close to the ground and dropping fast.

stem: The graph of a system of a linear and a quadratic equation is shown. Which system of equations is represented by the graph?
whyCorrect: Read each graph separately. The line goes through the origin and rises to the right, passing through about (1, 4), so its slope is positive: \( y = 4x \) . The parabola has its lowest point at (0, -8), which means the constant is -8, giving \( y = x^{2} - 8 \) . The x-intercepts near \( \pm 2.8 \) confirm it, since \( \sqrt{8} \approx 2.8 \) .

whyWrong.A: Both parts are wrong: a slope of -4 falls to the right, and \( x^{2} + 8 \) has its minimum at +8, so that parabola never crosses the x-axis.
whyWrong.B: The parabola is right, but \( y = -4x \) would slope down from left to right. The line shown rises.
whyWrong.C: The line is right, but \( y = x^{2} + 8 \) sits entirely above the x-axis, while the graph's parabola dips to -8 and crosses the axis twice.

stem: In 2000, a census was taken to determine the population of a certain town. The graph gives the estimated population y, in thousands, of this town x years after the 2000 census was taken, where 0 ≤ x ≤ 5. Based on the graph, which of the following is the closest to the estimated population 2 years after the 2000 census was taken?

stem: The graph of a system of a linear equation and a quadratic equation is shown. A solution to the system is \((x,y)\). What is a possible value of \(x\) ?
whyCorrect: A solution to a system is a point where the two graphs cross, so read off the \(x\)-coordinates of the intersection points, not anything about a single curve. The horizontal line meets the parabola at \(x=4\) and \(x=6\); of those, only 4 is offered.

whyCorrect: The solution of a graphed system is the point where the two lines cross, so read that point off the grid and report its second coordinate. The lines meet at \((-4, 2)\), so \(y = 2\). Do not read an intercept — the crossing point is what matters.

whyWrong.D: 3 is the \(y\)-intercept of the shallower line; the lines cross to the left of the \(y\)-axis, lower down.

stem:
Lucia and John will work together to make 60 paper flowers for a school party. The line shown represents the possible combinations of time, in hours, spent by Lucia and John to fulfill this task.
According to the graph, on average, how many paper flowers will Lucia make per hour?
whyCorrect: Use the intercept that isolates Lucia. The line meets the y-axis at (0, 12): John works 0 hours, so Lucia alone makes all 60 flowers, and it takes her 12 hours. Her rate is therefore 60 ÷ 12 = 5 flowers per hour. The slope of the line is not the answer — it compares the two people's times, not flowers per hour.

whyWrong.A: This is John's rate, from the other intercept: he alone finishes in 15 hours, and 60 ÷ 15 = 4.
whyWrong.C: 12 is the number of hours Lucia needs, not the number of flowers she makes in one hour. You still have to divide 60 by it.
whyWrong.D: 15 is the number of hours John needs, read off the wrong axis and left undivided.

note: Depends on a graph. Verified data for rebuilding it: a segment from (0, 12) to (15, 0); x-axis 'Time spent by John (hours)' 0 to about 17, y-axis 'Time spent by Lucia (hours)' 0 to about 15.

stem: Line \(n\) is shown in the xy-plane. Line \(k\) (not shown) is perpendicular to line \(n\). What is the slope of line \(k\)?
whyCorrect: First read line \(n\) off the graph: it crosses the y-axis at (0, 5) and the x-axis at (-1, 0), so its slope is \(\frac{5-0}{0-(-1)} = 5\). Perpendicular lines have slopes whose product is -1, so line \(k\) has slope \(-\frac{1}{5}\) — flip the fraction and change the sign, not one or the other.

whyWrong.B: You flipped and negated a slope of 6, which comes from misreading the y-intercept as 6 instead of 5.
whyWrong.C: 5 is the slope of line n itself. A perpendicular line cannot have the same slope.
whyWrong.D: This is a misread slope for n, and it is not perpendicular either.

note: Depends on a graph. Verified data for rebuilding it: line n passes through (0, 5) and (-1, 0), i.e. y = 5x + 5, drawn over roughly -2 <= x <= 1.5; grid spans x from -9 to 9 and y from -5 to 13.

stem: The function \(p\) is defined by \[ p(x) = -\frac{5}{8}x + \frac{21}{2}. \]What is the graph of \(y = p(x)\)?
whyCorrect: Two numbers settle it. The y-intercept is \(\frac{21}{2} = 10.5\), and the slope is \(-\frac{5}{8}\), so over the 10 units shown the line falls \(\frac{5}{8}(10) = 6.25\), landing at about 4.25 when x = 10. Only the graph that starts at 10.5 and ends near 4 does both.

whyWrong.A: This starts at 10.5 but drops all the way to 0 at x = 10, a slope of about -1, far steeper than \(-\frac{5}{8}\).
whyWrong.C: This starts at the right height but only falls to 8, a slope of about \(-\frac{1}{4}\) — too shallow.
whyWrong.D: The slope here is about right, but the line starts near 9.5 instead of 10.5, so the intercept is wrong.

note: All four answer choices are graphs, so this needs four figures, not one. Verified data: every choice is a segment drawn for 0 <= x <= 10 on axes with y from 0 to 13. A goes from (0, 10.5) to (10, 0); B (correct) from (0, 10.5) to (10, 4.25); C from (0, 10.5) to (10, 8); D from (0, 9.5) to (10, 3).

stem: A publishing company is preparing boxes of workbooks and textbooks for shipping. Each box of workbooks and textbooks will weigh a total of 40 pounds. The graph shown models the relationship between the number of textbooks x and the number of workbooks y that can be shipped in 1 box. Based on the graph, what is the weight, in pounds, of 1 textbook?
whyCorrect: Use the intercept that removes the workbooks. The line meets the x-axis at (10, 0): 10 textbooks and no workbooks fill a 40-pound box, so one textbook weighs 40 ÷ 10 = 4 pounds. Reading the y-intercept instead gives the workbook weight, which is not what is asked.

whyWrong.A: Negative weight is impossible; this comes from treating a slope or a difference of intercepts as a weight.
whyWrong.B: 10 is the number of textbooks that fill a box, not the weight of one. You still have to divide 40 by it.
whyWrong.D: 2 pounds is the weight of one workbook, from the y-intercept of 20: 40 ÷ 20 = 2. You read the wrong axis.

note: Depends on a graph. Verified data for rebuilding it: a segment from (0, 20) to (10, 0); x-axis 0 to about 13 (number of textbooks), y-axis 0 to about 23 (number of workbooks).

stem: Which is an equation of the graph shown?
whyCorrect: All four choices have slope 1, so the only thing to read off the graph is where the line crosses the y-axis. It crosses at (0, 3), so b = 3 and the equation is y = x + 3. As a check, the x-intercept at (-3, 0) satisfies it.

whyWrong.A: An intercept of 1 would put the crossing point at (0, 1), well below where the line actually meets the axis.
whyWrong.B: This crosses at (0, -1), below the origin; the graphed line crosses above it.
whyWrong.D: You took the x-intercept, -3, and used it as b. The y-intercept is the value of y when x = 0, which is +3.

note: Depends on a graph. Verified data for rebuilding it: the line y = x + 3 drawn over roughly -4 <= x <= 1; grid spans x from -4 to 1.5 and y from -1.5 to 4.5.

stem: How many solutions \((x, y)\) does the system of three linear equations represented in the graph have?
whyCorrect: A solution to the system has to satisfy all three equations at once, so it must be a point every line passes through. The two steep lines have the same slope and different intercepts, so they are parallel and share no point at all. It does not matter that the horizontal line crosses each of them — there is no point common to all three, so the system has 0 solutions.

whyWrong.B: There is no single point on all three lines; the two parallel lines never meet each other.
whyWrong.C: 2 counts the crossings visible on the graph (the horizontal line meets each steep line once). Those are intersections of pairs, not solutions of the three-equation system.
whyWrong.D: 3 assumes each pair of lines contributes a crossing, but the two parallel lines contribute none, and pairwise crossings are not solutions of the system anyway.

note: Depends on a graph. Verified data for rebuilding it: three lines, y = 6, y = 5x + 3, and y = 5x - 1.1 (x-intercept about 0.22), drawn on axes x from 0 to about 2.4 and y from 0 to 7.5.

stem: The graph of the linear equation \[ 15x + By = 60 \]is shown, where B is a constant. What is the value of B?
whyCorrect: Read the y-intercept off the graph — the line meets the y-axis at (0, 3) — and substitute that point into the equation: 15(0) + B(3) = 60, so 3B = 60 and B = 20. (The x-intercept is no help here: setting y = 0 gives 15x = 60, or x = 4, with B cancelling out entirely.)

whyWrong.A: \(\frac{3}{4}\) is the size of the line's slope, read off the graph rather than substituted into the equation.
whyWrong.B: 3 is the y-intercept itself. It is the value of y at that point, not the coefficient multiplying y.
whyWrong.C: 4 is the x-intercept, which is 60 ÷ 15 and tells you nothing about B.

note: Depends on a graph. Verified data for rebuilding it: the segment of 15x + 20y = 60 from (0, 3) to (4, 0); axes x from 0 to about 11 and y from 0 to about 7.

stem: Line \(k\) is shown in the xy-plane. Line \(n\) (not shown) is perpendicular to line \(k\) and passes through the point (2, 9). Which equation defines line \(n\)?
whyCorrect: Line \(k\) rises 2 for every 3 across — it passes through (-8, -8) and (4, 0) — so its slope is \(\frac{2}{3}\) and the perpendicular slope is \(-\frac{3}{2}\). That rules out C and D immediately. Then force the line through (2, 9): \(9 = -\frac{3}{2}(2) + b\) gives \(9 = -3 + b\), so b = 12.

whyWrong.A: The slope is right, but the intercept was found with the wrong sign: \(9 = \frac{3}{2}(2) + b\) gives 6. Substituting x = 2 into \(-\frac{3}{2}x\) gives -3, so b = 12.
whyWrong.C: This is the negative reciprocal with the sign left unchanged, so it is not perpendicular to k.
whyWrong.D: Same sign error on the slope, and (2, 9) does not satisfy it: \(\frac{3}{2}(2) - 3 = 0\), not 9.

note: Depends on a graph. Verified data for rebuilding it: line k is \(y = \frac{2}{3}x - \frac{8}{3}\), through (-8, -8) and (4, 0), drawn over roughly -11 <= x <= 9.5; grid spans x from -11 to 11 and y from -10 to 8.

stem: The graph of \(y = f(x)\) is shown. What is the y-intercept of the graph of \(y = f(x) + 13\)?
whyCorrect: Adding 13 to a function shifts every point up by 13, so the y-intercept moves up by 13 and stays on the y-axis. The graph shows f(0) = 1, so the new intercept is at (0, 1 + 13) = (0, 14). Only the y-value changes; x stays 0.

whyWrong.A: This subtracts 13 from 1 instead of adding. Adding a positive constant raises the graph.
whyWrong.C: This puts the 1 in the x-slot. An intercept on the y-axis always has x = 0; the 1 was the height, not a horizontal position.
whyWrong.D: This assumes f(0) = 0, reading the intercept at the origin. The line crosses the y-axis one unit above it.

note: Depends on a graph. Verified data for rebuilding it: the line y = 2.5x + 1, through (0, 1) and (-0.4, 0), drawn over roughly -2.8 <= x <= 2.1; grid spans x from -7 to 7 and y from -7 to 7.

stem: The graph of the linear equation \[ 8x + By = 56 \]is shown, where B is a constant. What is the value of B?
whyCorrect: The graph meets the y-axis at (0, 2), so substitute that point: 8(0) + B(2) = 56, giving 2B = 56 and B = 28. Do not use the x-intercept — setting y = 0 gives 8x = 56, i.e. x = 7, with B cancelling out, which is why the graph's x-intercept of 7 is only a consistency check.
note: Depends on a graph. Verified data for rebuilding it: the segment of 8x + 28y = 56 from (0, 2) to (7, 0), extended slightly past the x-intercept; axes x from 0 to about 10.5 and y from 0 to about 10.5.

stem: What is an equation of the graph shown?
whyCorrect: All four choices have the same intercept, 12, so the graph settles it on slope alone. The line falls as you move right, so the slope is negative, and it drops from 12 at x = 0 to 2 at x = 10 — 10 down over 10 across, a slope of -1.

whyWrong.A: Slope +1 rises to the right; the graphed line falls.
whyWrong.C: Slope 2 rises, and twice as steeply as the graph.
whyWrong.D: The sign is right but the line is twice too steep: a slope of -2 would reach y = -8 at x = 10, not y = 2.

note: Depends on a graph. Verified data for rebuilding it: the line y = -x + 12 drawn over roughly -4 <= x <= 10; grid spans x from -11 to 11 and y from -16 to 16.

stem: A certain open star cluster contains M-type stars and K-type stars. The estimated total mass of all M-type and K-type stars in this open star cluster is 132,778 quettagrams. The graph shown models the possible combinations of the number of M-type stars, x, and K-type stars, y, that could be in this open star cluster if all the M-type stars have the same estimated mass and all the K-type stars have the same estimated mass. Based on the graph, which of the following is closest to the estimated mass, in quettagrams, of each M-type star in this cluster?
whyCorrect: Use the intercept that removes the other kind of star. Where the line meets the x-axis there are no K-type stars, so about 160 M-type stars account for the entire 132,778 quettagrams: 132,778 ÷ 160 ≈ 830, closest to 828. The y-intercept would give the K-type mass instead.

whyWrong.B: 973 comes from the y-intercept of about 137: 132,778 ÷ 137 is the mass of one K-type star, not an M-type.
whyWrong.C: This is the total mass divided by about 2.5, or a slope misread; it is far too large for one star when 160 of them share the total.
whyWrong.D: This is roughly half the total mass, which would only be one star's mass if the cluster held two stars.

note: Depends on a graph. Verified data for rebuilding it: a segment from about (0, 137) to about (160, 0); x-axis 'Number of M-type stars' 0 to about 170, y-axis 'Number of K-type stars' 0 to about 165. The book's y-axis label misprints K-type as N-type.

stem: A hemisphere and a cone have circular bases of equal circumference and have been connected at their bases, as shown in the figure. The diameter of the base of the hemisphere is 6 centimeters (cm) and the total height of the figure is 9 cm. What is the total volume, in \(\text{cm}^3\), of the cone and hemisphere?
whyCorrect: Split the 9 cm of total height between the two solids. The radius is half of 6, so r = 3, and a hemisphere of radius 3 is 3 cm tall — that leaves 9 - 3 = 6 cm for the cone's height. Then the hemisphere is \(\frac{2}{3}\pi(3)^3 = 18\pi\) and the cone is \(\frac{1}{3}\pi(3)^2(6) = 18\pi\), for a total of \(36\pi\).

whyWrong.A: \(18\pi\) is just one of the two pieces; both happen to equal \(18\pi\), so stopping after one halves the answer.
whyWrong.C: \(45\pi\) comes from giving the cone the full 9 cm of height: \(\frac{1}{3}\pi(9)(9) = 27\pi\) plus \(18\pi\). The hemisphere occupies the top 3 cm.
whyWrong.D: \(162\pi\) treats the whole shape as a cylinder of radius 3 and height 9 × 2, or drops the \(\frac{1}{3}\) and \(\frac{2}{3}\) factors entirely.

note: Stem refers to a figure. Verified data for rebuilding it: a hemisphere (flat face down, radius 3 cm) sitting on top of a cone that points downward, sharing the circular base; a vertical dimension arrow at the right labelled 9 cm spanning the whole shape.

stem: The figure shown is a right circular cylinder with a radius r and a height of h. A second right circular cylinder (not shown) has a volume that is 576 times as large as the volume of the cylinder shown. Which of the following could represent the radius R, in terms of r, and the height H, in terms of h, of the second cylinder?
whyCorrect: In \(V = \pi r^2 h\) the radius is squared but the height is not, so scaling the radius by a and the height by b multiplies the volume by \(a^2 b\). Test the choices: \(8^2 \times 9 = 64 \times 9 = 576\), which is the required factor.

whyWrong.A: \(9^2 \times 8 = 648\), not 576. Here the larger factor was put on the radius, where squaring makes it too big.
whyWrong.B: \(9^2 \times 64 = 5{,}184\), nine times too large.
whyWrong.D: \(64^2 \times 9 = 36{,}864\). The 64 belongs to the squared effect of scaling the radius by 8, not to the radius itself.

note: Stem refers to a figure. It is only a generic labelled diagram: a right circular cylinder with a horizontal radius segment marked r on the top face and a vertical arrow at the right marked h. No measurements appear in it.

stem: The graph of \(y = f(x) - 1\) is shown. Which equation could define function \(f\)?
whyCorrect: The curve drawn is not f — it is f shifted down 1. It has a horizontal asymptote at y = 1 and passes through (0, 2), so the graphed function is \(2^x + 1\). Undo the shift by adding 1 back: \(f(x) = 2^x + 2\). Check it: \(f(0) - 1 = 3 - 1 = 2\), matching the graph.

whyWrong.A: \(2^x\) has asymptote y = 0 and passes through (0, 1); shifting it down would put the curve below the one shown by 2 units.
whyWrong.B: This shifts in the wrong direction twice; \(f(x) - 1 = 2^x - 2\), an asymptote at y = -2.
whyWrong.C: This is the equation of the curve shown, not of f. The graph is f minus 1, so f is one unit higher.

note: Depends on a graph. Verified data for rebuilding it: the curve \(y = 2^x + 1\) drawn for roughly -3.5 <= x <= 2.2, with horizontal asymptote y = 1 and passing through (0, 2); grid spans x from -3.5 to 3.5 and y from -1.5 to 5.5.

stem: The graph of the equation \(y = 2^x + k\) is shown, where k is a constant. What is the value of k?
whyCorrect: For \(y = 2^x + k\), the horizontal asymptote is y = k, because \(2^x\) shrinks to 0 as x runs left. The flat left tail of the graph sits at y = -7, so k = -7. Check it at x = 0: \(2^0 + k = 1 - 7 = -6\), and the curve does cross the y-axis at -6.

whyWrong.B: -6 is the y-intercept, which is \(1 + k\), not k itself. That extra 1 comes from \(2^0\).
whyWrong.C: A positive k would lift the whole curve above the x-axis; this graph lies mostly below it.
whyWrong.D: Same sign problem: with k = 6 the asymptote would be y = 6 and the curve would never reach negative values.

note: The book labels the four choices A, B, A, B; transcribed here as A, B, C, D in the order printed. Depends on a graph. Verified data for rebuilding it: the curve \(y = 2^x - 7\) drawn for roughly -11 <= x <= 4, with horizontal asymptote y = -7, y-intercept (0, -6) and x-intercept near x = 2.81; grid spans x from -11 to 11 and y from -11 to 11.

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y. A line of best fit for the data is also shown. For how many of the 9 data points is the actual y-value greater than the y-value predicted by the line of best fit?
whyCorrect: "Predicted" means the height of the line directly above or below that point's own x-value, so compare each point vertically with the line, not with the other points. The line runs from about (0.5, 80) up to about (10, 100). Going left to right, the points near x = 1, 2, 3, 4.5 and 9 sit above the line and the points near x = 5, 6, 7 and 8.5 sit below it. That is 5 points above.

whyWrong.A: 8 counts every point that is above y = 80, the line's starting height, instead of above the line at that point's own x. The line rises to 100, so being above 80 is not enough.
whyWrong.B: 7 comes from missing the two points on the right that sit just below the rising line; near x = 7 and x = 8.5 the line has already climbed past them.
whyWrong.D: 2 counts only the points that clear the line by an obvious margin. Three more points on the left are above it by a smaller amount and still count.

stem: The graph shows the number of internet users worldwide y, in billions, x years after 2007. Which of the following is closest to the number of internet users worldwide, in billions, 5 years after 2007?
whyCorrect: x is years after 2007, so "5 years after 2007" is x = 5, not the fifth plotted point counting from the left of a list. Go up from 5 on the horizontal axis to the point there and read across: it sits just under halfway between 2 and 3, about 2.4 billion.

whyWrong.A: 1.4 is the value at x = 0, that is, in 2007 itself.
whyWrong.C: 3.4 is higher than any plotted point; even at x = 9 the graph has only reached about 3.1.
whyWrong.D: 4.4 is well off the data, which never rises above about 3.

stem: The scatterplot shows data set A, which consists of the weights y, in pounds, of a Labrador retriever puppy at various ages, x, in months. The equation of a line of best fit for the relationship in data set A can be written as \( y = -5.1 + 8.7x \) , where \( 2 \le x \le 6 \) . The puppy was weighed again at 9 months old and weighed 52 pounds. Data set B consists of all the data points in data set A as well as the data point (9, 52). The equation of a line of best fit for data set B can be written as \( y = r + sx \) , where r and s are constants and \( 2 \le x \le 9 \) . Assuming the equations of the lines of best fit are calculated in the same way, which of the following is the best estimate for the value of s?
whyCorrect: s is the slope of the new line, so ask what the extra point does to the trend rather than trying to recompute a regression. Data set A's line predicts \( -5.1 + 8.7(9) = 73.2 \) pounds at 9 months, but the puppy actually weighed 52 pounds — far below the trend, and at the far right where it pulls hardest. A point that low on the right end drags the right side of the line down, so the new slope must be smaller than 8.7. Only 5.9 is smaller.

whyWrong.B: 8.7 is the old slope, which would only stay the same if the new point landed on the old line. It lands 21 pounds below it.
whyWrong.C: 13.8 is a steeper slope, which would require the new point to sit above the old line, not below it.
whyWrong.D: 17.7 is roughly double the old slope; nothing here makes the growth trend steeper. It also comes from dividing 52 by 3 or similar, which is not a slope.

note: The book prints the domains with the inequality signs reversed (2 ≥ x ≥ 6 and 2 ≥ x ≥ 9), which is impossible; transcribed as 2 ≤ x ≤ 6 and 2 ≤ x ≤ 9. The book also writes the new line as y = r + st, using t where the variable is x.

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y. A line of best fit is also shown. Which of the following equations best represents the line of best fit shown?
whyCorrect: The plotted line clearly rises from left to right, so its equation must contain an x term with a positive coefficient. Only one choice does. The others describe horizontal lines or are not equations at all, so no reading of the graph is needed beyond noticing the line is not flat.

whyWrong.A: y = 0 is the horizontal x-axis; the line shown is neither horizontal nor on the axis.
whyWrong.B: y = 1.7 is a horizontal line at height 1.7. A constant y cannot describe a line that climbs.
whyWrong.C: 0.7 is a number, not an equation, so it cannot represent any line. It is the slope-shaped part of choice D with the rest removed.

note: The line drawn in the figure passes close to the origin, so its y-intercept looks nearer 0 than the 1.7 in choice D; D is still the only choice that is an increasing linear equation. Choice C is printed without "y =".

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between t and d, along with a line of best fit. Which of the following equations is the most appropriate linear model for the data shown?
whyCorrect: Every choice has the same slope, so the slope tells you nothing — only the constant separates them. Test one point instead: the data run from about (230, 400) to about (270, 490). Substituting t = 230 into choice A gives \( -62.1 + 2.02(230) \approx 402 \) , which matches. The graph never shows t = 0, so the constant is far below the plotted d-values rather than near them.

whyWrong.B: At t = 230 this predicts about 627, roughly 200 too high; nothing on the graph reaches that.
whyWrong.C: At t = 230 this predicts about 822, nearly double the observed value. 357.8 was read as though it were a d-value on the graph.
whyWrong.D: At t = 230 this predicts about 857. Like C, it treats the constant as the height of the line over the plotted region instead of its value at t = 0.

stem: For the first 10 hours of an experiment, the scatterplot shows the temperature y, in degrees Fahrenheit (°F), of an object at various times x, in hours, since the start of the experiment. A line of best fit is also shown. Which of the following is the best interpretation of the slope of the line of best fit?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The predicted temperature increases at a constant rate of approximately 40°F per hour over the 10-hour period.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The predicted temperature decreases at a constant rate of approximately 40°F per hour over the 10-hour period.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The predicted temperature decreases at a constant rate of approximately 180°F per hour over the 10-hour period.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The predicted temperature increases at a constant rate of approximately 180°F per hour over the 10-hour period.

whyCorrect: Two decisions: direction and size. The line rises left to right, so the rate is an increase, which rules out half the choices immediately. For the size, the line climbs from roughly 200°F at 0 hours to roughly 550°F at 10 hours, a rise of about 350°F over 10 hours, so about 35°F per hour — approximately 40.

whyWrong.B: The direction is wrong. A decrease would need the line to fall as time increases, and it rises.
whyWrong.C: Both parts are wrong: the line rises, and 180°F per hour would put the object above 1,800°F by hour 10.
whyWrong.D: The direction is right but the size is not. 180 is roughly the height of the line near the start, or its rise over 2 hours, not its rise per single hour.

stem: The scatterplot shows 5 measurements of the body length, in centimeters (cm), of a New Zealand fur seal from an age of 1 year to 6 years old. A line of best fit is also shown. For a New Zealand fur seal at an age of 3 years old, what is the body length predicted by the line of best fit, to the nearest 10 cm?
whyCorrect: The question asks for the line's value, not a data point's, and at age 3 there is no plotted point — that is the trap. Go up from 3 on the horizontal axis to the line itself and read across: the line is a little above 105, so to the nearest 10 cm the prediction is 110.

stem: The scatterplot shows 5 measurements of the body length, in centimeters (cm), of a New Zealand fur seal from an age of 1 year to 6 years old. A line of best fit is also shown. For a New Zealand fur seal at an age of 3 years old, what is the body length predicted by the line of best fit, to the nearest 10 cm?
whyCorrect: Read the line, not the points: at age 3 no seal was measured, so trace up from 3 to the line of best fit and across to the vertical axis. The line is just above 100 there, so to the nearest 10 cm the predicted length is 100 cm.
note: The book truncates the last words of the stem to "to the nearest ?"; the rounding unit is restored as 10 cm from the parallel question printed beside it. If a different unit was intended the answer changes.

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between x and y for the 10 data points in data set A. Data set B is created by multiplying the y-value of each data point from data set A by 40. Which of the following equations is the most appropriate model for data set B?
whyCorrect: First model data set A itself: the points pass through about (0, 3), (2, 20), (3, 43) and (4, 100), which fits \( y = 5(2.04)^{x} \) . Multiplying every y-value by 40 scales the whole output, so it multiplies the coefficient in front, not the exponent or the base: \( 40 \times 5 = 200 \) , giving roughly \( y = 200(2.04)^{x} \) . Only one choice has a coefficient anywhere near 200.

whyWrong.A: This is the model for data set A itself, before the y-values were multiplied by 40.
whyWrong.B: This multiplies the wrong thing. Scaling y by 40 does not turn the coefficient 5 into 40, and it does not add a constant 40 either.
whyWrong.C: Adding 40 shifts every point up by 40; multiplying by 40 stretches them. At x = 4 data set B is near 4,000, and this predicts about 127.

note: Choice D carries a spurious additive 2.04; the exact transformed model is 200(2.04)^x, and D is the only choice with a coefficient of that size.

stem: The line graph shows the number of customers who visited a restaurant each day during a four-day period in the summer. According to the line graph, for which day during this four-day period did the restaurant have the smallest number of customers who visited?
whyCorrect: Smallest number of customers means the lowest point on the graph, not the leftmost or the shortest gap between points. The graph rises from left to right the whole way, so the lowest point is the first one, Day 1, at about 22 customers.

whyWrong.B: Day 2 is slightly higher than Day 1, at about 27. It is close, but the graph still climbs between the two.
whyWrong.C: Day 3 is around 47, well above the start.
whyWrong.D: Day 4 is the highest point, about 56 — the largest number of customers, not the smallest.

stem: A group of 10 gardeners recorded data on the germination rates of their tomato crop for one growing season. The scatterplot shows the relationship between the number of tomato seeds planted, x, and the number of tomato seeds that germinated, y, for each of the gardeners. A line of best fit is also shown. Which of the following is the best interpretation of the slope of the line of best fit in this context?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The number of tomato seeds planted is predicted to increase by 60 seeds every 100 days.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The number of tomato seeds planted is predicted to increase by 300 seeds every 100 days.

choices.label: C

whyCorrect: A slope always says how much the vertical variable changes per unit of the horizontal variable, so here it is germinated seeds per seed planted — time is not a variable in this graph at all.
